GUIDE TEXT
# How do you care for a snake plant in the UAE?
Dracaena trifasciata (syn. Sansevieria trifasciata). Also called: Sansevieria, Mother-in-law's tongue, Viper's bowstring hemp, لسان الحماة, نبتة الثعبان.

Snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata, also sold as Sansevieria) is one of the easiest plants for UAE homes and offices. Give it bright indirect light; it also copes with dim corners. Water only when the soil is fully dry, often every 2–3 weeks in summer under AC and every 4–6 weeks in winter. Use a pot with drainage holes. Overwatering kills most snake plants.

## Quick facts
- Light: Bright indirect is best; copes with low light. Gentle morning sun is fine, harsh summer sun is not.
- Water, Apr–Oct: When the soil is fully dry: often every 2–3 weeks under AC
- Water, Nov–Mar: When the soil is fully dry: often every 4–6 weeks
- Temperature: Prefers 15–24 °C. Copes with summer heat in shade if the soil dries out. Protect from below 10 °C.
- Humidity: Prefers lower humidity. In humid coastal homes, water less often.
- AC tolerance: High. Keep 1 m away from a direct vent.
- Outdoors in UAE: Yes, in shade. Avoid midday sun May–Sep and cold inland nights.
- Pets: Toxic to cats and dogs if chewed; keep away from young children
- Difficulty: Easy, good for beginners
- Size indoors: 30–120 cm depending on variety
- Growth: Slow

## How much light does a snake plant need?
A snake plant grows best in bright, indirect light, such as 1–2 metres from an east- or north-facing window. It also survives in low light (a dim hallway, an office corner, a bedroom with curtains), but it grows very slowly there and the leaf colour fades.
In the UAE, the risk is too much sun, not too little. Afternoon sun through west- or south-facing glass in summer burns the leaves and leaves pale or brown dry patches that never recover. A sheer curtain is enough to stop it.
- Tip: Turn the pot a quarter turn every month so the leaves grow straight.
- Tip: A room with no window at all is too dark, even for a snake plant.

## How often should you water a snake plant in Dubai?
Water only when the soil is completely dry all the way down. Push a finger or a wooden skewer into the pot: if any soil feels damp, wait. Indoors under AC this is often every 2–3 weeks from April to October and every 4–6 weeks from November to March, but treat these as starting points, not a schedule. Small or terracotta pots in a warm, bright spot dry much faster; large pots in a dim AC room stay dry for longer.
In humid coastal homes and after rain, soil dries slowly, so water less often. Inland, dry heat and hot wind dry pots quickly, so check outdoor pots more often in summer.
When you water, water thoroughly until it runs out of the drainage hole, then empty the saucer after 15 minutes. Never leave the pot standing in water.
UAE tap water is desalinated and then remineralised, and its mineral content varies by area and building. If you see a white crust on the soil or pot, or brown leaf tips, flush the pot with plenty of water to wash the salts out, or switch to filtered water.
- Tip: Water the soil, not into the centre of the leaf rosette. Water sitting there can rot the base.
- Tip: When in doubt, wait another week. A thirsty snake plant recovers; a waterlogged one often does not.

## What soil and pot does a snake plant need?
Use a fast-draining mix: a cactus and succulent soil, or regular potting soil mixed half and half with perlite or coarse sand. Heavy, water-holding garden soil keeps the roots wet and leads to rot.
Always use a pot with a drainage hole. Decorative pots without holes are fine as an outer cover, as long as you lift the inner pot out to drain. Terracotta and cement pots dry faster than plastic or glazed ceramic, which helps prevent overwatering.

## Should you fertilise a snake plant?
Snake plants need very little feeding. From March to October, give a balanced fertiliser at half the strength on the label once a month. Do not feed from November to February, when growth slows down.
Too much fertiliser causes brown leaf tips and salt build-up, so less is better than more.

## When should you repot a snake plant?
Repot every 2–3 years, or when roots come out of the drainage hole or the pot starts to bulge or crack. Snake plants like a snug pot, so go up only one size (about 3–5 cm wider).
The best time in the UAE is October–November or February–April. After repotting, wait about a week before watering so any damaged roots can heal.

## How do you propagate a snake plant?
Division is the easiest and fastest method: take the plant out of the pot, cut through the root mass so each piece has leaves and roots, and pot each piece separately.
You can also root leaf cuttings. Cut a leaf into 8–10 cm sections, let them dry for 2–3 days, then stand them upright (bottom end down) in damp succulent soil or in water. Roots take 4–8 weeks. Note that cuttings from yellow-edged varieties usually grow back plain green; only division keeps the yellow edge.

## Where should you place a snake plant at home or in the office?
Snake plants suit bedrooms, living-room corners, office desks and reception areas because they tolerate lower light and AC rooms year-round. A bathroom with a window works well too.
Avoid spots directly under an AC vent, next to a sunny glass wall, or on a balcony in summer without shade. Tall varieties make good floor plants beside a sofa or TV unit; compact types like 'Hahnii' and the starfish snake plant suit shelves and desks.
When moving a plant between an AC room and the outdoors, do it gradually over a week or two (a few hours in shade at first), and never straight from AC into full summer heat or sun.

## Care through the UAE year
- Summer (May–Sep): Indoors under AC it keeps growing slowly: water when the soil is dry, often every 2–3 weeks. Keep it out of direct sun through glass. Outdoor plants need full shade; check the soil every few days in heatwaves, especially small or terracotta pots.
- Autumn (Oct–Nov): Best time to repot, divide and move plants back to balconies and terraces (gradually, starting in shade). Feed once a month until the end of October.
- Winter (Dec–Feb): Growth slows down. Water less, often every 4–6 weeks, and stop feeding. Coastal winter nights are mild enough. Inland (Al Ain, desert areas) and in Riyadh or Kuwait, nights can fall below 10 °C: move outdoor plants to a sheltered spot or indoors on cold nights. Make sure outdoor pots drain after rain.
- Spring (Mar–Apr): Start feeding again once a month. A good second window for repotting. Move outdoor plants into shade before May.

## Common problems
### Why are my snake plant leaves turning yellow and soft?
Yellow, soft or mushy leaves almost always mean overwatering and root rot. The soil stays wet, the roots suffocate and begin to rot from the base upward.
How to tell: Soil still damp days after watering, a soft or dark base, a sour smell from the pot.
1. Stop watering.
2. Take the plant out of the pot and remove all soil.
3. Cut off every black, mushy root and any rotten leaves with clean scissors.
4. Let the plant dry in the shade for 1–2 days.
5. Repot in fresh, dry succulent soil in a pot with a drainage hole.
6. Wait one week before the first watering.
### Why are my snake plant leaf tips turning brown?
Brown, dry tips usually come from salt and mineral build-up from hard tap water or too much fertiliser. Long dry spells followed by heavy watering, or cold air blowing from an AC vent, cause it too.
How to tell: Crispy brown tips, sometimes with a white crust on the soil or pot rim.
1. Flush the soil with plenty of water and let it drain fully.
2. Switch to filtered water, or let tap water stand overnight.
3. Cut fertiliser to half strength, March–October only.
4. Move the plant away from AC vents.
5. Trim the brown tips with clean scissors, following the natural leaf shape. Cut tips do not grow back.
### Why are my snake plant leaves wrinkled or curling?
Wrinkled, thin or curling leaves mean the plant is not getting enough water. Either the soil has been bone dry for too long, or rotten roots can no longer take water up.
How to tell: Dry soil pulling away from the pot edge (thirst), or wet soil with a soft base (root damage).
1. If the soil is dry, water thoroughly. Leaves should firm up within a week.
2. If the soil is wet, check the roots and treat as root rot (see above).
### Why is my snake plant falling over?
Leaves that bend, flop or fall outward are weak from overwatering or from too little light, which makes them grow tall and thin. A top-heavy plant in a light plastic pot can also tip over.
How to tell: Leaves bend at the base, look stretched, or the whole plant leans.
1. Check that the soil dries between waterings.
2. Move the plant to brighter indirect light.
3. Tie floppy leaves loosely together for support, or remove damaged leaves at the base.
4. Repot into a heavier terracotta or cement pot if it keeps tipping.
### What are the pale or brown dry patches on my snake plant?
Pale, bleached or brown papery patches are sunburn. This is common in the UAE when a plant sits in afternoon sun behind glass, or outdoors in summer without shade.
How to tell: Dry patches on the side facing the window or the sun, appearing within a few days of a move.
1. Move the plant out of direct sun or add a sheer curtain.
2. The damaged patches will not heal. Leave them, or remove badly burnt leaves at the base.
### What is the white cotton at the base of my snake plant leaves?
White, cottony clusters between the leaves are mealybugs, a sap-sucking pest. They hide deep in the leaf base and spread to nearby plants.
How to tell: White fluff, sticky residue, slow growth, yellowing spots.
1. Move the plant away from other plants.
2. Wipe off the bugs with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
3. Spray the whole plant, especially the leaf bases, with a neem-based spray once a week for 3–4 weeks.
### Why are there tiny flies around my snake plant?
Small black flies around the soil are fungus gnats. They breed in soil that stays wet, so they are a sign of overwatering.
How to tell: Tiny flies rising from the soil when you touch the pot.
1. Let the soil dry out completely before watering again.
2. Cover the soil with a 1–2 cm layer of sand or small pebbles.
3. Yellow sticky traps catch the adults.
### Why is my snake plant not growing?
Snake plants are naturally slow, and in low light or in winter they can stop growing for months. That is normal and not a sign of a problem as long as the leaves stay firm and green.
How to tell: No new leaves for several months, but healthy-looking existing leaves.
1. Move it to brighter indirect light.
2. Feed once a month from March to October.
3. Be patient. New shoots usually appear in spring and autumn.

## FAQs
Q: How often should I water a snake plant in Dubai?
A: Water only when the soil is completely dry. Indoors under AC that is often every 2–3 weeks from April to October and every 4–6 weeks from November to March, but check the soil first: small pots and warm, bright spots dry faster, big pots in dim AC rooms slower.
Q: Is a snake plant good for the bedroom?
A: Yes. It copes with low light and AC rooms, needs little care, and unlike most plants it takes in carbon dioxide at night. One plant will not noticeably change the air in a room, but it is one of the most practical bedroom plants.
Q: Is a snake plant safe for cats and dogs?
A: No. Snake plants contain saponins, which can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea if a pet chews the leaves. Keep the plant out of reach of pets and young children, and call your vet if your pet eats any.
Q: Can a snake plant live outside in the UAE?
A: Yes, in shade. Outdoors it grows well from October to April. From May to September keep it in full shade, out of the midday and afternoon sun, and check the soil every few days in heatwaves, because pots dry out fast. Move it outside gradually, not straight from an AC room. In winter it is happy on the coast, but inland and in colder GCC cities protect it from nights below 10 °C.
Q: Can a snake plant grow in water?
A: It can be kept in water with only the roots submerged, and leaf cuttings root in water. Change the water every week and keep the leaves dry. In water it grows more slowly and less reliably than in free-draining soil, so pot it up if it starts to struggle.
Q: Does a snake plant need sunlight?
A: It needs some daylight, but not direct sun. Bright indirect light is best; it survives in dim corners but grows very slowly. Direct summer sun in the UAE burns the leaves.
Q: Does a snake plant flower?
A: Occasionally. Mature plants that have been pot-bound for a while can send up a stalk of small, fragrant, greenish-white flowers that open in the evening. It is a sign of a healthy, slightly root-bound plant.
Q: How long does a snake plant live?
A: With basic care a snake plant lives for many years, and it keeps producing new shoots that you can divide into new plants.
Q: Why is a snake plant a popular gift in the UAE?
A: It is almost impossible to kill, looks good in modern homes and offices, and in feng shui it is seen as protective and bringing good energy. That makes it a common housewarming, Eid and corporate gift.
Q: Can a snake plant live in a room with no window?
A: Only with good artificial light. Under bright LED or office lighting that is on most of the day it survives, but grows very slowly. In a room that stays dark it slowly weakens, so give it a few weeks near a window from time to time.
Q: Does a snake plant clean the air?
A: Not noticeably in a normal room. Studies that found snake plants removing chemicals were done in small sealed chambers, and a home would need far more plants than anyone keeps to match fresh air from ventilation. Buy it because it looks good and is easy to keep, not as an air filter.
Q: Should I mist my snake plant?
A: No. Snake plants do not need misting, and water that collects in the centre of the leaves can rot the base. Instead, wipe dust off the leaves with a damp cloth every month or two so they can take in light.
Q: What is the difference between the snake plant varieties?
A: They all need the same care. 'Laurentii' has yellow leaf edges. 'Zeylanica' has dark green leaves with lighter grey-green bands and no yellow edge. 'Hahnii' is a compact rosette for desks and shelves. The starfish snake plant (Sansevieria cylindrica 'Starfish') has thick, round leaves that fan out like a starfish.
Q: Which snake plant size should I buy?
A: PlantsWorld measures height from the bottom of the nursery pot to the tip of the tallest leaf. A mini or starfish snake plant suits desks and shelves, a 50–80 cm plant suits side tables and consoles, and a tall plant of 100 cm or more works as a floor plant in a corner or beside a sofa.
Q: Should I order my snake plant in the nursery pot or a decorative pot?
A: The plant is the same. Choose the black nursery pot if you want the lowest price or will repot into your own planter. Choose a decorative pot if you want it ready to display: it arrives fully potted with soil mix, perlite and a drainage layer at the base.
Q: How do I water a snake plant that came in a PlantsWorld decorative pot?
A: Water only when the soil is fully dry, as with any snake plant. If the pot has a drainage hole, water until it runs out and empty the saucer. If it has no hole, give less water each time so it never collects at the bottom; the drainage layer gives a little room, but it does not replace a hole.
